steps.say: Adult scores mislead in children, so use the paediatric activity index at every visit. Six simple items, from pain to blood to night waking, add up to a number that dictates admission or rescue. Below ten means quiet disease, the middle bands track mild and moderate flares, and sixty five or more declares severe colitis. Score it yourself rather than trusting memory, because the number changes management that same day.
steps.tx: Apply the **PUCAI scoring system** (Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis Activity Index, a six-item gut score) at each review. PUCAI below 10 indicates remission; 10-34 mild; 35-64 moderate; and 65 or above defines acute severe colitis. Its items cover abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, stool consistency and frequency, nocturnal waking and activity limitation. Record the score trend across visits, since a rising PUCAI predicts steroid failure earlier than symptoms alone suggest.

steps.say: Childhood colitis behaves nothing like the adult version, so expect widespread disease from day one. Six to eight out of ten children present with inflammation spanning the whole colon right up from the rectum. That pancolitis pattern raises cancer and growth stakes for decades ahead. The comparison diagram here pins the distinction: ulcerative colitis stays continuous and mucosal, starting at the rectum, while Crohn disease skips and burrows deep.
steps.tx: Expect **pancolitis predominance in children** at presentation. Extensive colitis or pancolitis (E4 by Paris classification, the paediatric extent label) occurs in over 60-80% of pediatric patients with ulcerative colitis, far higher than in adults. Continuous rectal-onset mucosal disease distinguishes it from the skip lesions and transmural injury of Crohn disease shown alongside. Extent sets surveillance intensity and surgical counselling, so map it with full colonoscopy plus terminal ileum views at diagnosis.

vis.alt: Diagram comparing mucosal continuous ulcerative colitis with transmural Crohn disease, including skip lesions, noncaseating granulomas, fissures, and fistulas.

steps.say: Mesalazine remains the workhorse for mild to moderate disease, but children need weight based doses, not adult tablets halved by guess. Aim sixty to eighty milligrams per kilo daily by mouth, capped near five grams, and add a nightly rectal dose for stubborn rectal disease. The topical treatment reaches where tablets cannot. Check adherence honestly at every visit, because missed sachets explain most so called failures.
steps.tx: Dose using **mesalazine dosing in mild-moderate UC** precisely. Oral 5-aminosalicylate (mesalazine, the topical gut anti-inflammatory) at 60-80 mg/kg/day (maximum 4.8 g/day) combined with topical rectal 5-ASA (25 mg/kg/day) is first-line induction and maintenance. Rectal therapy treats tenacious proctitis (rectal inflammation) that oral drug never reaches. Continue maintenance indefinitely after remission, since stopping invites relapse, and monitor renal function yearly on chronic high dose therapy.

steps.say: A child with severe colitis can deteriorate frighteningly fast, so admit on the number, not on how brave they look. Sixty five or more on PUCAI means a bed, a plain abdominal film to exclude megacolon, and intravenous methylprednisolone without delay. Dose one to one and a half milligrams per kilo daily, capped at sixty, split in two doses. Keep the child nil by unnecessary poking too: stool tests, bloods and surgical awareness from hour one.
steps.tx: Apply **acute severe colitis management** as an inpatient emergency. Patients with PUCAI of 65 or above require immediate hospitalisation, abdominal radiography (plain film to exclude toxic dilation), and intravenous methylprednisolone at 1-1.5 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg/day) in 2 divided doses. Add thromboprophylaxis (clot prevention), correct anaemia and albumin, stop antidiarrhoeals, and involve surgeons early even when colectomy feels distant, because delay kills options.

steps.say: Steroids do not get forever to work; the calendar forces the next move. Recheck PUCAI on day three, and a score still above forty five warns that steroids will fail. By day five, sixty five or more demands rescue without further waiting. Choose infliximab infusion or ciclosporin drip according to infection screen, drug history and surgical backup. Dithering past day five trades a planned rescue for an emergency colectomy.
steps.tx: Apply the **Day 3 and Day 5 rescue decision** rule strictly. PUCAI score above 45 on Day 3 of IV steroids predicts steroid failure, so prepare rescue logistics early; PUCAI of 65 or above on Day 5 mandates second-line rescue therapy with infliximab (5-10 mg/kg infusion, the anti-TNF antibody) or intravenous ciclosporin (the calcineurin inhibitor drip). Screen stools for infection before rescue, check thiopurine history and varicella immunity, and keep colectomy counselling parallel, since rescue buys the colon one chance, not immunity.

steps.say: Toxic megacolon is the complication you must never miss overnight. Suspect it when a severely ill child stops passing stool yet the belly balloons with tenderness and fever. Confirm non obstructive transverse colon dilation beyond fifty six millimetres after age ten, or forty in younger children, plus systemic toxicity. Stop all motility drugs instantly, decompress, correct electrolytes, and summon surgeons before perforation.
steps.tx: Diagnose by the **toxic megacolon diagnostic threshold** on plain film plus clinical toxicity. Toxic megacolon is defined as non-obstructive transverse colon dilatation above 56 mm in children over 10 years (or above 40 mm in younger children) accompanied by systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, anaemia and altered consciousness). Exclude perforation with erect views, withhold narcotics and anticholinergics, roll the child regularly to redistribute gas, and escalate to colectomy if dilation or toxicity progresses despite 24 to 72 hours of maximal care.

steps.say: Years of pancolitis quietly raise cancer risk, so surveillance starts on schedule, not on symptoms. Begin chromoendoscopy screening eight to ten years after diagnosis, sampling every segment with dye spray. Bring that first screen forward to diagnosis itself when sclerosing cholangitis coexists, since that combination accelerates dysplasia. The chronic injury poster here, with pseudopolyps and lead pipe change, shows exactly the mucosa you are watching.
steps.tx: Time **colorectal cancer surveillance timing** by extent and comorbidity. Screening colonoscopy with chromoendoscopy (dye spray magnified examination) is initiated 8-10 years post-diagnosis in pediatric pancolitis, or immediately at diagnosis if coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis is present. Take segmental biopsies for dysplasia (precancerous change) even from flat mucosa, because cancers in colitis hide without lumps. Shorten intervals after dysplasia, strictures or strong family history, and never discharge pancolitic children from surveillance.

vis.alt: Comparison poster. The ulcerative colitis side shows colon-only continuous disease from the rectum, a lead-pipe colon, friable mucosa and pseudopolyps, crypt abscesses, crypt architectural distortion, and inflammation limited to mucosa and submucosa.
vis.caption: Crypt abscesses and crypt architectural distortion are the biopsy changes drawn on the colitis side. Basal plasmacytosis is not labelled. Illustration: StewardMD.

steps.say: When drugs cannot hold the colon, or dysplasia appears, surgery cures the gut disease itself. Removing the entire colon and rectum with a J shaped ileal pouch joined to the anus ends colitis permanently while preserving continence. Children return to school, sports and normal growth afterward. Counsel honestly about pouchitis and fertility effects, but present the pouch as liberation from a failing colon, not defeat.
steps.tx: Offer **surgical indication and restorative proctocolectomy** decisively when indicated. Restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA or J-pouch, a reservoir fashioned from small bowel joined to the anus) is the curative surgical treatment of choice for medically refractory disease or dysplasia. Indications include failed rescue therapy, toxic megacolon unresponsive to care, growth failure from chronic disease, and confirmed dysplasia. Operate electively with experienced pouch surgeons whenever the child stabilises, since planned pouches outperform emergency ones.
